criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural drinking-water service access in Ndiass and two neighboring villages (Samkédj and Mbayar) in Senegal, including public standpipes, private household connections, community connections, water pricing/affordability, non-payment disconnections, and service interruptions.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines an institutional, regulatory, and contractual governance reform of rural motorized boreholes (RÉGEFOR). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly analyzes concrete rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) utility licensing and delegated private management/maintenance contracting structures (ASUFOR operating license, contrat de gérance, contrat de maintenance hydraulique), (2) mandatory metered volumetric full-cost-recovery tariff rules (vérité des prix / tarification au coût complet, borehole tariff classes FC1–FC3, cross-subsidized private connection vs. public building tariffs), (3) formal disconnection enforcement rules requiring shutoff for non-payment, and (4) street-level discretion and accommodation by ASUFOR and the delegated manager (debt forgiveness and below-cost tariffs for schools/community buildings; informal installment, advance, and arrears accommodations to avoid disconnecting insolvent households), as well as contractual/administrative complexity and lack of regulatory arbitration.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative socio-legal/sociological case study supplemented by operational quantitative data and source triangulation, based on two rounds of primary fieldwork in Ndiass (May 2006 and May–July 2009), stakeholder interviews, and utility billing/consumption records.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service-access outcomes: network and connection expansion (from 6 public standpipes in 1999 to 370 water points including 320 private connections in 2006 serving 8,000 inhabitants), volumetric water consumption (450 m3/month in Mbayar vs. 578 m3/month or 48.16 L/person/day in Ndeing), tariff/affordability changes (price doubled from 5 to 10 FCFA per 25L basin), billing recovery and arrears (63% recovery rate; 445,700 FCFA / 2,294 m3 unpaid arrears including 195,200 FCFA across 297 private connections), discretionary avoidance of household disconnections, and a two-day service outage during a maintenance contract dispute.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and multi-level units of analysis (borehole user association ASUFOR of Ndiass, 8,000 rural residents across Ndiass, Samkédj, and Mbayar, and user connection categories), the institutional/rule-type exposure (RÉGEFOR reform), concrete access outcomes, and the qualitative case-study design with embedded operational records.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in French. Per Inclusion Criterion 10, non-English/Portuguese/Dutch studies are eligible when translation from the provided full text is feasible and the study is potentially important; French-to-English translation from the complete 23-page text is directly feasible and this study provides rich empirical evidence on rural tariff, disconnection, and discretionary accommodation mechanisms (log translation method and translator in extraction_note during data extraction).

evidence_quotes.quote: Jusqu’à son adhésion à la réforme, en décembre 1999, le village ne disposait que de six bornes-fontaines publiques. En 2006, il comptait 370 points d’eau dont 320 branchements privés.

Un premier travail de recueil des données s’est déroulé en mai 2006 dans le cadre d’enquêtes de terrain pour notre thèse. Un second travail de recueil a eu lieu entre mai et juillet 2009, au moment de la restitution des résultats de recherche, pour compléter et actualiser ces données de terrain.

En application du principe de la tarification au coût complet - coût de la consommation effective auquel s’ajoute une fraction des coûts fixes -, l’Asufor de Ndiass a été obligée d’augmenter le prix de l’eau - de 5 FCFA à 10 FCFA la bassine - dans un milieu rural où 65,2% des individus et 57,5% des ménages vivent en dessous du seuil de pauvreté

Les normes de gestion imposées stipulent que le gérant doit couper l’eau à tout usager en défaut de paiement. Mais ce dernier préfère trouver un compromis qui peut avoir des effets pervers sur la pérennité du service.
À défaut d’être prise en compte dans le montage institutionnel de la réforme, la dimension sociale de l’accès à l’eau est gérée, de manière discrétionnaire par l’Asufor et le gestionnaire délégué.
L’Asufor a été obligée d’accepter puisque les populations sont restées deux jours sans eau.

raw_response.exposure: Senegal's RÉGEFOR rural water reform (1999 onward): formal licensing of borehole user associations (ASUFOR), delegated private management and exclusive private maintenance contracts, shift from flat-rate to metered full-cost-recovery volumetric tariffs, formal disconnection rules for non-payment, and street-level discretionary accommodations for arrears.
raw_response.outcome: Drinking-water network and private connection expansion (from 6 public standpipes to 370 water points including 320 private connections serving 8,000 residents), household/village water consumption (m3/month and L/person/day), tariff affordability (doubling from 5 to 10 FCFA/basin), payment arrears and recovery rate (63% recovery; 445,700 FCFA arrears), discretionary non-disconnection of insolvent users, and a two-day water service interruption.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural borehole user association (ASUFOR) and served population of 8,000 inhabitants across the village of Ndiass (5,000 inhabitants in 8 neighborhoods) and two neighboring villages, Samkédj (2,000 inhabitants) and Mbayar (1,000 inhabitants), in the Thiès region of Senegal (including 360–370 distribution points / 297–320 private household connections).
raw_response.rationale: Empirical socio-legal/sociological case study (with embedded utility billing and consumption data from 2006 and 2009 fieldwork in Ndiass, Senegal) examining how rule-type legal, regulatory, and tariff mechanisms under Senegal's RÉGEFOR rural water reform—specifically licensed user associations (ASUFOR), delegated private management and maintenance contracts, mandatory metered full-cost-recovery tariffs, formal non-payment disconnection rules, and informal street-level discretion/accommodation—affect household water connections, consumption quantities, affordability, arrears, disconnections, and service continuity. Full text is in French and directly translatable per Inclusion Criterion 10. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative socio-legal case study supplemented with descriptive quantitative operational/billing records and interviews (fieldwork in May 2006 and May–July 2009)
